items.stimulus:
Early travellers who visited the fictional islands of the Teral archipelago described the gift exchanges they saw as generosity, pure and simple. Later fieldworkers reached a different view. Among the Velau, the islanders they studied, a gift is never quite free. Accepting a basket of yams creates a debt that the receiver is expected to repay, but not immediately and not with the same thing. Returning an identical basket the following morning would be taken as an insult: it signals that the receiver wishes to close the account and end the relationship. A proper return comes months later, is slightly larger or different in kind, and so places the original giver in debt in turn.

On this account, the point of exchange is not the goods themselves but the bond that unpaid obligations sustain. A household that owes nothing to anyone is, in Velau terms, a household with no allies. Refusing a gift is also serious, since it amounts to declining the relationship that the gift proposes.

Some anthropologists warn against treating this as a universal law. They note that in many market societies people deliberately separate gifts from trade: a dinner guest who offered the host cash would cause offence, precisely because payment settles a debt instantly. Yet even there, the critics concede, people keep rough mental records of who invited whom, and a friendship in which one side always gives tends to fade. The difference, they argue, may lie less in whether reciprocity exists than in how openly it may be acknowledged.
items.question: Which one of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.text: The Velau regard refusing a gift as less serious than returning an identical gift the next morning.

A weather balloon is filled at ground level, where the air pressure is 100 kPa and the temperature is 27 °C (300 K); its volume there is 6 m³. items.question: What is the volume of the balloon at an altitude of 9 km?

options.text: 4.5 m³
6 m³
8 m³
10 m³
15 m³

items.explanation_ko: 1) 지상에서 PV/T = 100×6÷300 = 2이므로 어느 고도에서든 V = 2T÷P이다. 2) 9 km: T = −48+273 = 225 K, P = 30 kPa. 3) V = 2×225÷30 = 450÷30 = 15 m³. 어림 요령: 압력이 100→30으로 3/10이 되면 부피는 10/3배, 온도가 300→225 K로 3/4이 되면 부피는 3/4배이므로 6×(10/3)×(3/4) = 15. 오답: A 온도 변화만 반영(6×225/300). B 부피가 변하지 않는다고 본 값. C 3 km 행을 읽은 값. D 6 km 행을 읽은 값. 유형 팁: 기체 관계식은 먼저 상수(PV/T)를 구해 두면 행마다 한 번의 계산으로 끝난다. → 정답 E

items.stimulus:
Determinism is the view that every event, including every human decision, is the inevitable result of earlier causes operating according to the laws of nature. If determinism is true, then given the exact state of the world a century before you were born, the choice you made at breakfast this morning could not have been otherwise. Many people find this conclusion alarming, because it seems to leave no room for free will, and without free will it is hard to see how anyone could deserve praise or blame.

Philosophers who accept this reasoning are called incompatibilists: they hold that free will and determinism cannot both be true. Some of them conclude that, since we are plainly free, determinism must be false. Others accept determinism and conclude that free will is an illusion.

Compatibilists reject the starting point. They argue that the incompatibilist has misunderstood what freedom means. On the compatibilist view, to act freely is not to act without any cause; it is to act from one's own desires and reasoning, without being forced or prevented by outside pressures. A woman who hands over her wallet because a robber is pointing a knife at her does not act freely. A woman who hands over her wallet to a charity collector because she wants to support the cause does act freely, even if her generosity has causes in her upbringing and temperament. What matters is the kind of cause, not whether there is one.

Critics reply that this simply changes the subject. If the donor's desires were themselves fixed by events long before she was born, they ask, in what sense are those desires 'her own'? Compatibilists answer that desires do not need to come from nowhere to belong to a person; they need only be desires the person would endorse on reflection. Whether that answer satisfies depends largely on what we wanted from the idea of freedom in the first place.

items.stimulus:
From the thirteenth century onwards, merchants from towns along the Baltic and North Sea coasts, led by Lübeck, gradually formed an association that came to be known as the Hanseatic League, or Hansa. It was never a state. It had no permanent army, no single ruler and, for long periods, no fixed list of members. What held it together was a shared interest in trade and a set of privileges that its merchants had won in foreign ports.

These privileges were remarkable. In cities such as London, Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod, Hanseatic merchants lived and worked in walled trading posts known as kontors. Within these compounds they were often governed by their own rules rather than by local law, and they sometimes paid lower customs duties than even local traders did. To rulers, granting such terms could make sense: the Hansa brought grain, timber, furs, fish and wax that their own merchants could not easily supply, and the duties it did pay were a reliable source of income.

The Hansa defended its privileges chiefly through economic pressure. When a ruler threatened them, member towns might agree to stop trading with that territory altogether. Because many regions depended on Hanseatic shipping for essential goods, such boycotts were often effective, and on occasion the towns also went to war.

Yet the same arrangements carried the seeds of decline. Local merchants resented foreigners who paid less tax than they did, and as kings built stronger, more centralised states, they became less willing to tolerate enclaves outside their control. Meanwhile, Dutch and English shippers became able to supply the same goods themselves. A boycott works only if the other side has nowhere else to buy. By the end of the sixteenth century, most of the kontors had lost much of their special status, and the League faded not through a single defeat but through the slow loss of the conditions that had made it useful.

Imagine two drivers, Ines and Marek, who each glance at a text message while driving through a quiet suburb. Each takes their eyes off the road for the same three seconds. In that moment a child runs into the road in front of Marek's car, and he cannot stop in time. No one steps in front of Ines, and she arrives home without incident. Most people judge Marek far more harshly than Ines, and the law usually agrees: Marek may face a serious charge, while Ines, if she is caught at all, receives a fine.

Philosophers call this pattern 'moral luck': the tendency to judge people by outcomes that lay outside their control. It is worth asking whether the pattern can be justified. Ines and Marek made exactly the same choice, with exactly the same knowledge and the same disregard for other people's safety. The only difference between them is the presence of a child, something neither driver chose or could have foreseen. If blame is meant to reflect what a person did and why, it is hard to see how a fact that neither of them controlled can make one of them more blameworthy than the other.

This does not mean that the outcome is morally irrelevant. Marek has caused harm that he must try to repair, and it is fitting that he should feel a kind of grief that Ines need not feel. But owing repair is not the same as deserving more blame. When a storm blows a tree from one garden onto a neighbour's fence, nobody is to blame, yet the owner of the tree may still be expected to help rebuild the fence.

If we took this seriously, we would judge Ines more harshly than we now do, rather than judging Marek more gently. Her carelessness was just as dangerous; she was simply fortunate.

Imagine two drivers, Ines and Marek, who each glance at a text message while driving through a quiet suburb. Each takes their eyes off the road for the same three seconds. In that moment a child runs into the road in front of Marek's car, and he cannot stop in time. No one steps in front of Ines, and she arrives home without incident. Most people judge Marek far more harshly than Ines, and the law usually agrees: Marek may face a serious charge, while Ines, if she is caught at all, receives a fine.

Philosophers call this pattern 'moral luck': the tendency to judge people by outcomes that lay outside their control. It is worth asking whether the pattern can be justified. Ines and Marek made exactly the same choice, with exactly the same knowledge and the same disregard for other people's safety. The only difference between them is the presence of a child, something neither driver chose or could have foreseen. If blame is meant to reflect what a person did and why, it is hard to see how a fact that neither of them controlled can make one of them more blameworthy than the other.

This does not mean that the outcome is morally irrelevant. Marek has caused harm that he must try to repair, and it is fitting that he should feel a kind of grief that Ines need not feel. But owing repair is not the same as deserving more blame. When a storm blows a tree from one garden onto a neighbour's fence, nobody is to blame, yet the owner of the tree may still be expected to help rebuild the fence.

If we took this seriously, we would judge Ines more harshly than we now do, rather than judging Marek more gently. Her carelessness was just as dangerous; she was simply fortunate.

and stands a moment in the dark, quite still.

waves from his car. She lifts her hand. That's all.

items.stimulus:
Many people assume that peer review, the practice of sending a manuscript to independent experts before publication, is as old as science itself. In fact, its history is shorter and more uneven than that. When Philosophical Transactions first appeared in London in 1665, under licence from the Royal Society, it was largely the personal project of its editor, who chose what to print himself. In the following century the Society set up a committee to decide which papers it would publish, but its members judged papers among themselves rather than seeking outside opinions.

Written reports from named referees became more common during the nineteenth century, as learned societies multiplied and the number of submissions grew. Even then, practice varied widely. Many editors continued to accept papers on their own authority, especially from authors they knew and trusted. As late as the 1930s, a famous physicist was reportedly offended when an American journal sent his paper to an anonymous reviewer, a practice he had not met in the European journals where he usually published.

The system familiar today spread mainly after the Second World War. Governments were funding research on a vastly greater scale, the number of scientists rose sharply, and editors could no longer be experts in every topic they received. Sending papers to outside specialists became a practical necessity rather than a mark of distinction. By the later twentieth century, a paper that had not been peer reviewed was widely regarded as not quite part of the scientific record.

This history matters for current debates. Critics point out that reviewers often miss errors, that they may favour work which confirms their own views, and that review slows the spread of findings. Defenders reply that an imperfect filter is better than none. Both sides sometimes speak as though peer review were the timeless foundation of scientific reliability. Yet science made great advances for centuries without peer review in its modern form, relying instead on replication, open correspondence and public dispute. Peer review is better understood as one tool among several, adopted to solve a particular problem of scale, and it should be judged by how well it solves that problem today.

items.stimulus:
When I started my first job as a junior engineer, I learned more from overhearing my supervisor's phone calls than from any training course. I heard how she calmed an angry client, how she admitted a mistake to her manager and how she refused an unrealistic deadline. Nobody planned these lessons. They happened because we sat three metres apart.

This kind of learning is now disappearing. Since many firms adopted remote and hybrid working, junior staff spend much of their week alone at a kitchen table, and the casual lessons that once filled an office day no longer reach them. A video call is scheduled, has an agenda and ends when the agenda does. No one overhears anything.

Defenders of remote work point out that it saves commuting time, widens the pool of applicants and helps parents balance work and family. These benefits are real, and I do not wish to deny them. But they fall mostly on experienced staff, who already have their networks and skills. The costs fall on beginners, who have not yet learned what they do not know and therefore cannot ask about it.

The evidence from my own firm is striking. Last year, junior employees who chose to work mainly from home were promoted at half the rate of those who chose to come into the office most days. Remote work, it seems, is quietly holding back a generation of young professionals.

Some managers try to fill the gap with formal mentoring schemes, such as monthly video meetings between a junior and a senior colleague. These are better than nothing, but they replace a constant stream of small observations with an occasional conversation. A beginner who watches an expert handle twenty problems learns something different from one who hears about two of them a month later.

Firms do not need to abandon flexible work. But they should recognise that mentoring was never just a scheme; it was a side effect of sharing a room. If they want the next generation to learn, they must give junior staff good reasons to be in the same room as the people they are learning from.

items.stimulus:

Speaker 3 (Halima Strand, potter): My bowls are used every day, for soup and rice and fruit. If they are beautiful, that beauty is part of their usefulness, not a holiday from it.

items.question: Speaker 3's view most directly challenges which assumption made by Speaker 1?

items.stimulus: To estimate the number of trout in a lake, ecologists catch 60 trout, mark each with a small tag and release them. items.question: Using the Lincoln-Petersen formula, what is the estimated number of trout in the lake?
items.explanation_ko: 1) N = (M × C) ÷ R = (60 × 80) ÷ 12. 2) 60 ÷ 12 = 5를 먼저 계산하면 5 × 80 = 400. 오답: B M × R ÷ C로 변수를 바꿔 넣은 값(60 × 12 ÷ 80). C 두 포획 수를 더하고 재포획 수를 뺀 값(60 + 80 − 12). D R로 나누지 않은 값(60 × 80). 유형 팁: 나눗셈이 깔끔하게 떨어지는 쌍(60 ÷ 12)을 먼저 약분하면 계산이 빨라진다. → 정답 A
